qualitative-predictor.def: A predictor whose values are categories (levels), such as region or student status; it enters a regression through dummy variables.

dummy-variable.def: A 0/1 indicator column that is 1 for one level of a factor and 0 otherwise.

one-hot.def: Machine-learning name for coding a categorical variable as 0/1 dummy columns, one per level (one is dropped when the model has an intercept).

baseline.def: The level of a factor that has no dummy variable; the intercept is its mean, and every dummy coefficient is a difference from it.

interaction.def: When the effect of one predictor depends on the value of another; modelled by adding the product \(X_1X_2\) as a predictor.

main-effect.def: A predictor's own term (e.g. \(\beta_1X_1\)) as opposed to an interaction term built from it.

residual-plot.def: Residuals plotted against fitted values (or a predictor, or time). A good model shows no pattern.

heteroscedasticity.def: Non-constant variance of the error terms; seen as a funnel shape in a residual plot.

wls.def: Least squares in which each squared residual is multiplied by a weight, usually the inverse of that observation's error variance.

outlier.def: An observation whose response is far from the value predicted by the model (a large residual).

studentized-residual.def: A residual divided by its estimated standard error; values beyond about ±3 suggest an outlier.

leverage.def: How unusual an observation's predictor values are; in simple regression \(h_i=\frac1n+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\sum(x_{i'}-\bar x)^2}\). Average leverage is \((p+1)/n\).

collinearity.def: Two or more predictors closely related to each other; it inflates the standard errors of their coefficients.

multicollinearity.def: Collinearity among three or more predictors, possibly with no single pair highly correlated.

vif.def: \(1/(1-R^2_{X_j|X_{-j}})\): how much collinearity inflates the variance of \(\hat\beta_j\). 1 is the minimum; above 5–10 is a problem.

power.def: The probability that a test correctly rejects a false null hypothesis, e.g. detects a non-zero coefficient.

knn-regression.def: Predict at \(x_0\) by averaging the responses of the K training points nearest to \(x_0\).

curse-dimensionality.def: In many dimensions a fixed number of observations becomes sparse, so the 'nearest' neighbours are far away and local methods like KNN perform poorly.
